chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Chu Berry and how Horace turned his riff into 'Christopher Columbus'
summary: Chu Berry joined Fletcher from Teddy Hill's band and died in a Conneaut, Ohio crash. Horace built 32 bars from Chu's riff at the Roseland, tried it out with Claude Hopkins and had a hit.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Huh! There's another legend. That fellow was a great guy.

And the first thing I can say about him is the town of Conneaut, Ohio, should pay tribute to him always. That's where Conyard, Ohio, (inaudible) attributed to his death. You know he had that accident and got killed down there. And Chu traveled with Fletcher's band. In fact, Fletcher got Chu out of a great little band out of New York called Teddy Hill, in which Chu played the Savoy Ballroom. And Chu Berry was a legend. He as fat and big as he was, and could lift if a whole band, (inaudible), he could play, and he went to Chicago in that Chicago band with Fletcher, and Roy Eldridge and that bunch "Christopher Columbus" (inaudible) at the Grand Terrace in those days. And we fan mail broadcasted there, and, of course, had his (inaudible), and he was a guy that used to play a real riff -- which turned out to be Christopher Columbus, because Chu would play some Bop-ta-ta-

In a thing. One day, I said, "Hey ta-ta-ta, ta-ta, and then go off from there, (Inaudible), Chu." That got to be a little pet rhythm riff of his. I say, "I like this thing, man. We were at the Roseland Ballroom when this happened, and I said, Hey, you mind me making a tune out of this thing? I think I can make 32 bars out of it." He said, "I don't care. Go ahead, you know." So, sure enough, I made this thing.

I first took it up to the Cotton Club when Carl Hopkins was playing. He played it down there, and he went crazy over it. I said, "Well, Carl, I'll bring it back." I took it up, I took it down to Roseland and told Chu what I'd done, Fletcher (Inaudible) took it downstairs, and the guys went -- everybody could read -- came back upstairs and played this thing, and I had the trumpets counter point going against it -- (Inaudible) just a do-ee-da-ta-ta -- weird, you know? Went upstairs and when I started it it was an instant hit thing.
